sources.title: Night Moves: Is the Overnight Drift the Grandmother of All Market Anomalies?
sources.what_it_measured: Independent sceptical quantification, 1995-2022; dates the waning of the effect to around 2012 following a half dozen papers published 2008-2015, and argues the cross-sectional version is not tradeable after costs and borrow.

contradictory_evidence: The contradictory evidence IS the entry - this is the rare case where the original authors published the refutation themselves, in a Fed venue, with a named mechanism for the death. Elm Wealth independently dates the waning earlier, to around 2012, which if right means even the RFS sample's later years were already decaying. Glasserman, Krstovski, Laliberte & Mamaysky (arXiv 2507.04481, 2025) add that overnight returns do not significantly predict intraday returns once news-topic exposure is controlled, and conclude that 'because of the extreme turnover required to trade the over-intra effect, our findings fall short of being a viable trading strategy'. There is no serious dissent in the other direction.
our_inference: Our inference is that this entry's value to the lab is no longer as an alpha source but as the cheapest available NEGATIVE CONTROL, and the lab should run it as such before spending trials on anything else in this file. The reasoning: the effect is precisely specified (one hour, one instrument, a known sign, a known magnitude of 1.48 bps per day), it is known to have been large through 2020 and known to be zero from 2021, and the lab's sample is entirely inside the dead period. The lab's bar files carry the full 23-hour session (about 1380 one-minute bars per day, confirmed in data/futures/ES.parquet), so the 02:00-03:00 ET window is directly available. If the lab's pipeline reports a significant positive drift in that hour over 2025-06 to 2026-09, the pipeline has a bug or a lookahead - because the people who discovered the effect say it is not there. That is a rare and valuable thing: a pre-specified null with an authoritative expected answer, on the lab's own instrument, costing one afternoon. Given that research/experiments_futures.jsonl already contains one retraction for a lookahead in opening_range_pos that silently produced survivors, a calibration test of this kind is worth more than another hypothesis.
proposed_mechanism: Whatever remains of the mechanism is inventory compensation: dealers who absorb a one-sided closing imbalance carry the position overnight and are paid for the risk as European liquidity arrives and lets them unwind. The reason it died is not that dealers stopped wanting compensation but that the imbalance they had to absorb halved, because execution algorithms now slice closing orders finely enough that no single dealer ends the day materially long or short. That is a durable structural change, not a cycle, which is why we expect the effect to stay dead.
observable_variables: the 02:00-03:00 ET hourly return from 1m closes, on the full 23-hour bar file
the same for every other hour of the 24-hour cycle, as the control
the volume in the 15:45-16:00 ET bucket relative to trailing average, as an available proxy for closing imbalance intensity
calendar year, to split 2025 from 2026
failure_conditions: Inverted relative to the other entries, because the expected result is zero. The entry 'fails' in the informative sense if the 02:00-03:00 ET mean return over the lab's sample is significantly POSITIVE at |t| > 2 - that outcome should be treated as evidence of a pipeline defect (lookahead, roll contamination, timezone error, survivorship in the contract stitching) before it is treated as evidence of alpha. It fails in the boring sense, confirming the Fed's finding, if the mean is indistinguishable from zero, which is what we expect.
data_we_lack: Nothing. Note one trap specific to this window: 02:00-03:00 ET spans the US/Europe daylight-saving mismatch twice a year, and the Frankfurt/London open moves relative to ET on those dates. The window must be defined in ET as the papers do, but the lab should check whether the effect concentrates differently in the weeks when London and New York are offset. Roll boundaries must also be excluded, as with VR-03.
falsification_test: On ES and NQ over the full sample, compute the mean return of every one-hour bucket of the 24-hour cycle with Newey-West errors, and report the 02:00-03:00 ET bucket against the other 23. Pre-register the expectation that it is zero. Run this before any other test in this file.
cost_feasibility_note: For completeness, the historical magnitude in lab units: 1.48 bps per day is 1.13 ES points ($56.50) against a 0.326-point cost, i.e. costs 29% of gross; and 4.35 NQ points ($87.00) against 0.689 points, costs 16% of gross. Both would have passed the lab's 60% gate comfortably in the 1998-2020 sample. The expected magnitude in the lab's actual sample is zero, which is why expected_magnitude_points is set to 0.0 rather than to the historical figure. This is also the clearest single illustration for the lab of the difference between a published magnitude and a forward-looking one.
why_this_might_be_wrong: High confidence here means high confidence that the effect is DEAD, which is the claim being made. The objection to my framing is that a negative control is only as good as the alternative hypothesis it rules out: if the lab's pipeline finds nothing at 02:00-03:00, that is consistent with a correct pipeline AND with a pipeline so broken it finds nothing anywhere. A negative control should therefore be paired with a positive one - a synthetic series with a known injected edge - and I am recommending only half of the pair. The second objection is that the Liberty Street piece is a blog post rather than a peer-reviewed paper, though it is by the original authors on their own result, which is about as good as refutations get.

name: Volatility compression predicts the SIZE of the next move and not its sign - the cleanest negative result in the territory
source_claim: Singha, 'Hidden Order in Trades Predicts the Size of Price Moves' (arXiv 2512.15720, Nov 2025), using SPY second-resolution data over 36 sessions and 38.5 million trades, computes an order-flow entropy from a 15-state Markov transition matrix. Conditioning on entropy below the 5th percentile raises the subsequent 5-minute absolute return by a factor of 2.89 (t = 12.41, p < 1e-4); the lowest-versus-highest entropy quintile magnitude ratio is 2.17. Directional accuracy over the same conditioning is 45.0% with p = 0.12 - statistically indistinguishable from chance. The author's own framing is that entropy is invariant under sign permutation, so it cannot by construction carry directional information. Independently, Preethi (SSRN 6316139, 2026), clustering NIFTY 5-minute bars with UMAP and HDBSCAN over calendar 2025, finds regime-conditioned forecasts cut 30-minute realised-volatility MSE by about 5.65% and states that 'volatility-related features differ significantly across regimes, while return differences remain statistically insignificant - regime organization is primarily volatility-driven rather than drift-driven.'

sources.title: Data-Snooping, Technical Trading Rule Performance, and the Bootstrap
sources.what_it_measured: 7,846 technical rules including channel breakouts and filter rules over 100 years of DJIA under White's Reality Check; on the S&P 500 FUTURES contract specifically, no evidence that the best technical rule outperforms once data snooping is accounted for.

contradictory_evidence: The contradictory evidence runs the other way here: the vendor literature is uniformly positive and uniformly worthless. Every claim we found about NR7, narrow-range, inside days, Bollinger squeezes and 'volatility contraction patterns' predicting directional breakouts traces to Toby Crabel's 1990 trade book and is currently carried by screener and indicator vendors. The one quantified claim located - a 90.77% success rate for VCP breakouts when major indices trade above their monthly 10-period EMA - has no stated sample, no definition of success, no cost model and a survivorship-prone universe. We found no peer-reviewed evidence that range compression predicts direction, and we looked for it deliberately. Park & Irwin's survey of 95 modern technical-analysis studies (Journal of Economic Surveys 21(4), 2007) found 56 positive but concluded that most are compromised by data snooping, ex post rule selection and inadequate cost estimation, and their own Reality-Check test of US futures 1985-2004 found no general profitability.
our_inference: Our inference is that the lab should stop treating compression as a directional setup and start treating it as the one reliable input it actually is: a forecast of the SIZE of the next move. That matters here more than it would elsewhere, because the lab's binding constraint is a fixed dollar cost divided by a variable dollar capture. A magnitude forecast with a 2-to-3x conditioning ratio does not create an edge, but it does let a marginal edge be deployed only where the denominator of the cost ratio is largest, and switched off everywhere else - which is exactly the VR-02 mechanism generalised, and exactly the thing the prior 240-trial grid could not express, because every one of its 818 rows was a single feature with a single threshold and a single direction. We also infer, from the Singha result specifically, that the lab should add a magnitude-prediction diagnostic to its funnel alongside the direction test: a feature that predicts |return| with a t of 12 and direction with a t of 1.5 is not a failed signal, it is a correctly-working volatility filter that has been mislabelled.
proposed_mechanism: Low entropy in the order flow, and narrow realised range, both indicate that one side is quietly accumulating or that liquidity has thinned to the point where little volume moves price far. Both states resolve into a larger move when the accumulation completes or when the thin book is hit. Neither state contains information about WHICH way, because the state is defined on a quantity that is symmetric in the sign of returns - the same narrow range arises before an up-move and a down-move. It persists because it is not an inefficiency at all: it is a property of how order flow arrives, and there is nothing to arbitrage.
observable_variables: realised range over a trailing window relative to its own trailing distribution: (high-low over last N bars) / (median of that quantity over the last 20 sessions at the same minute-of-day)
realised volatility over a trailing 30-minute window, deseasonalised by minute-of-day
the ratio of the trailing 30-minute realised volatility to the trailing 120-minute realised volatility, which is a compression measure scale-free in the level of volatility
volume over the trailing window relative to the same minute-of-day's trailing average
the target for the magnitude test: absolute return over the next 30 or 60 minutes
failure_conditions: As a magnitude forecaster it fails if the bottom quintile of the compression measure does not raise the subsequent 30-minute absolute return by at least 1.5x relative to the top quintile on ES and NQ - the published SPY ratio is 2.17 to 2.89 and anything below 1.5x is not worth conditioning on. As a direction signal it is ALREADY falsified by the sources and by the lab's own prior grid, and we are asserting in advance that a directional test on it will return a hit rate indistinguishable from 50%; if the lab runs that test and finds otherwise, we would suspect the test before we believed the result.
data_we_lack: The Singha entropy measure needs trade-level data with a state classification, which requires tick data the lab does not have; the 1m OHLCV range-compression proxy is a weaker substitute and the 2.89x conditioning ratio should not be expected to survive the downgrade. Databento sells CME tick history cheaply (about $42 per quarter for MNQ per the Mesfin study) if the lab ever wants the stronger version, but we would test the OHLCV proxy first.
falsification_test: On ES and NQ 1m bars, compute the deseasonalised compression ratio (trailing 30-minute RV over trailing 120-minute RV), sort all intraday observations into quintiles, and report the mean absolute forward 30-minute return by quintile together with the directional hit rate by quintile. Two numbers decide it: the bottom-to-top magnitude ratio must exceed 1.5, and the hit rate must NOT differ from 50% - the second is a confirmation that we understand the mechanism, and a hit rate materially different from 50% would mean something other than compression is being measured.
cost_feasibility_note: expected_trades_per_session is deliberately 0.0 and expected_magnitude_points is null: this entry generates no trades of its own. Its economic value is entirely as a multiplier on other entries' cost ratios. Quantified against VR-01: the lab's measured cost is fixed at 0.326 ES points and 0.689 NQ points per round turn, so a conditioning variable that raises the mean absolute payoff-window move by 1.6x (which is what we measured for the first-30-minute volatility tercile: 5.90 to 9.42 ES points) improves any dependent strategy's gross-to-cost ratio by the same 1.6x at zero marginal cost. That is a larger improvement than moving from MES to MNQ (3.1x) can be stacked with, and the two are multiplicative.
why_this_might_be_wrong: My strongest objection is Cederburg, O'Doherty, Wang & Yan. Their result is that conditioning on volatility state looks excellent in a spanning regression and then loses to the unconditional strategy in real time, because the conditioning weights are estimated with error and the relationship is structurally unstable. Everything I have written about conditioning in VR-02 and here is vulnerable to exactly that critique, and the honest position is that a real-time, trailing-window, no-lookahead implementation of a volatility filter may well underperform simply not filtering at all. The second objection is that the magnitude conditioning I measured in the lab's own data is partly mechanical - volatility clusters, so of course a volatile morning predicts a volatile afternoon - and a mechanical amplitude gain does nothing for a strategy with no edge.

name: Pre-announcement volatility compression, and the announcement-day risk premium
source_claim: Two separate claims, both requiring a release calendar. First, the lull: Bomfim, 'Pre-Announcement Effects, News Effects, and Volatility' (Journal of Banking & Finance 27(1), 2003, from Fed FEDS working paper 2000-50), fitting a GARCH model to daily S&P 500 returns over June 1989 - December 1998 (N = 2,414), finds that the day before a scheduled FOMC announcement carries a conditional-volatility coefficient of -0.486 with t = -7.80, roughly HALF normal conditional volatility, while the announcement day itself carries +0.79 with t = 2.73, about 40% above normal. Critically the pre-announcement calm appears only after 1993, when the Fed began announcing decisions on meeting days, so it is caused by the scheduling rather than being a calendar artifact. Zhu (BIS Working Paper 1079, 2023) adds that turnover falls before FOMC announcements and rises afterward, and that 'on average, one third of the pre-FOMC price drift can be attributed to the volume dynamics and liquidity shocks'. Second, the premium: Savor & Wilson (JFQA 48(2), 2013), over 1958-2009, find 11.4 bps average excess return on scheduled announcement days (CPI, employment, FOMC) against 1.1 bps on all other days, more than 60% of the annual equity risk premium, with a Sharpe roughly ten times higher on announcement days.

sources.author_or_org: Kurov, Sancetta, Strasser & Wolfe (JFQA 54(1); ECB WP 1901)
sources.what_it_measured: Second-by-second E-mini S&P 500 price impact per one-standard-deviation surprise over [release, release+5min], Jan 2008 - Mar 2014: nonfarm employment 0.420% (R2 0.50), ISM 0.240%, CPI -0.111% (R2 0.15), PPI 0.013% and insignificant (R2 0.00).

sources.title: Rent Seeking by Low-Latency Traders
sources.author_or_org: Chordia, Green & Kottimukkalur (Review of Financial Studies 31(12), 4650-4687)
sources.what_it_measured: SPY and ES respond to announcement surprises within five milliseconds with a hundredfold rise in trading intensity; total profits from trading quickly are roughly $50,000 per event for SPY/ES, market-wide, and have not grown even as speed has.

contradictory_evidence: Substantial, and it kills the directional half of this territory. The pre-FOMC announcement drift - the most famous claim in this area, Lucca & Moench's 49 bps in the 24 hours before the release with t > 4.5 - collapsed out of sample: Kurov, Wolfe & Gilbert (Finance Research Letters 40, 2021), on E-mini S&P 500 futures, report 49.2 bps (t = 4.60) for Sept 1994 - March 2011 and 4.7 bps (t = 0.78) for April 2011 - December 2019. It survived 2011-2015 only on press-conference meetings (44.5 bps, t = 3.35) and fell to 9.2 bps (t = 1.33) on press-conference meetings in 2016-2019 - and since January 2019 EVERY FOMC meeting has a press conference, so the one conditioning variable that kept it alive is now degenerate. The FOMC-cycle even-week effect (Cieslak, Morse & Vissing-Jorgensen, Journal of Finance 2019) is worse: Uppal (2025), with data through 2023, reports week-0 daily returns of +13.6 bps (t = 2.76) in the 1994-2016 replication and -13.9 bps (t = -1.58) in the true out-of-sample 2017-2023 window - a sign flip - with the in-sample result halving when two days are dropped, and the proposed mechanism (leaks after biweekly Board meetings) institutionally discontinued in 2004. On the lull itself, Bollerslev, Li & Xue (Review of Economic Studies 85(4), 2018) find that in the final 30 minutes before an announcement volume and volatility tick UP slightly, not down; that is not a contradiction of Bomfim so much as a horizon distinction - the lull is a days-to-hours phenomenon and the final half hour is a ramp - but conflating the two would produce the wrong trade.
our_inference: Our inference is that this territory yields one usable thing and one usable thing only, and it is not directional. The usable thing is the lull: a scheduled, calendar-known, ex-ante identifiable state in which conditional volatility is roughly halved. For a lab whose problem is that gross capture is too small relative to a fixed cost, a predictable HALVING of volatility is a predictable halving of every mechanism's gross-to-cost ratio, and the correct response is to not trade those sessions at all. That is a turnover reduction obtained for free from a calendar, and it is the mirror image of VR-02. Separately, the Savor-Wilson announcement-day premium is the one effect in this entire file whose cost arithmetic is not close: 11.4 bps is 8.7 ES points or 33.5 NQ points against costs of 0.326 and 0.689 points, so costs are 3.7% and 2.1% of gross, on roughly 30 events a year. We flag honestly that this is beta timing rather than alpha - you capture it by being long on those days - and that it requires holding the cash session or overnight rather than an intraday round turn. Finally: everything about trading the release itself is closed to this lab. Prices respond within five milliseconds, the entire market-wide latency prize is about $50,000 per event, and the sign of the equity response to good news inverts with the business cycle (Andersen, Bollerslev, Diebold & Vega find good news lowering stocks in expansion and raising them in recession), so any surprise-to-direction mapping fitted on our sample would be fitted to one regime and would invert in the next.
proposed_mechanism: Before a scheduled release, informed traders have nothing to trade on that the release will not reveal in minutes, and uninformed traders rationally defer discretionary trades until the uncertainty resolves. Volume falls, and with it volatility. After the release the information is public and the repositioning happens at once. The announcement-day premium is the compensation investors require for bearing the risk of the resolution itself: risk is concentrated on those thirty days, and so is the reward. Both persist because both are consequences of the release schedule being public, which is the opposite of the condition under which an effect gets arbitraged away.
observable_variables: a release calendar table keyed on (release_name, date, time_et) - the acquisition is the work here, see below
a binary is_day_before_FOMC flag and a binary is_announcement_day flag
minutes-until-next-release and minutes-since-last-release as continuous features
realised volatility of the session, to verify the lull empirically before relying on it
for the premium: the session or overnight return on flagged days
failure_conditions: The lull fails if, once the calendar is built, the median realised volatility of pre-FOMC sessions in the lab's own 2025-2026 sample is not materially below that of matched control sessions - Bomfim's coefficient implies roughly half, and anything above 0.85x is not worth acting on. The premium fails if the mean excess return on the roughly 30-45 announcement sessions in our sample is not positive; note in advance that with n around 40 and a session standard deviation of 61 bps, the standard error on an 11.4 bps mean is about 9.7 bps, so our sample CANNOT resolve this effect - a null here is uninformative and must not be recorded as a refutation.
data_we_lack: A release calendar with dates AND times in ET. This is the only genuine data acquisition in the whole file, and it is smaller than it sounds - roughly three to four hours of work against free official sources, which are the ground truth that vendors themselves scrape. Concretely: BLS publishes yearly release-schedule list views with times to the minute in ET (CPI, PPI, Employment Situation, ECI, JOLTS), scrapeable at bls.gov/schedule/{YYYY}/{MM}_sched_list.htm; BEA publishes a machine-readable JSON schedule plus ICS and RSS (GDP, Personal Income and Outlays/PCE) and is the best-engineered of the sources; Census covers Advance Retail Sales, Durable Goods and Housing Starts on a standard 08:30 ET; and the FOMC time is a deterministic rule rather than a scrape - 14:15 ET from Sept 1994 to March 2011, 12:30 or 14:15 from April 2011 to January 2013, and 14:00 ET since March 2013, with the press conference at 14:30 and, since January 2019, at every meeting. FRED's fred/releases/dates endpoint gives dates but explicitly NOT times, so it is useful only as a completeness cross-check; ALFRED gives vintages, needed if the lab ever wants first-print values to construct surprises, but no clock times. The lab's existing FMP key may cover FMP's economic-calendar endpoint, which does return datetimes in UTC, but vendor calendars are notorious for minute-level timestamp errors and the whole exercise is worthless if the minute is wrong - cross-check twenty CPI and NFP rows against BLS before trusting it. Verdict: worth building, but for the lull and for hygiene, not for alpha.
falsification_test: Build the calendar table, then run one test: compare the distribution of session realised volatility on pre-FOMC days against matched control days (same day-of-week, nearest in calendar time, no other release) across ES and NQ. A ratio at or above 0.85 kills the lull as an actionable filter. Do NOT run a directional test on the pre-FOMC window; the out-of-sample record above makes that a known-dead hypothesis and spending trials on it would inflate the family's multiple-testing threshold for no reason.
cost_feasibility_note: The announcement-day premium is the only figure in this file that clears costs by more than an order of magnitude: 11.4 bps is 8.7 ES points ($437) against $16.28, costs 3.7% of gross; 33.5 NQ points ($670) against $13.78, costs 2.1%; MES $43.70 against $2.47, 5.7%; MNQ $67.00 against $1.72, 2.6%. At roughly 30 events a year that is 0.12 round turns per session, the lowest turnover of any entry here. But the honest accounting is that this is a long-only beta exposure on selected days, not a market-neutral edge, and its Sharpe comes from concentrating the same equity premium into fewer days rather than from creating return. The lull, by contrast, has no gross capture at all - its entire value is in the trades it prevents, and a filter that removes the lowest-amplitude 8% of sessions from a strategy whose costs are fixed is worth roughly the cost of those trades.
why_this_might_be_wrong: The strongest objection is sample size, and it applies to both halves. The lab's fifteen-month sample contains about eleven FOMC meetings and perhaps forty scheduled major releases in total. Bomfim's lull was estimated on 2,414 days and Savor & Wilson's premium on 51 years. Neither can be confirmed or refuted on our data, which means building the calendar buys the lab a feature it must take on faith from the literature rather than one it can validate locally - and taking effects on faith from the literature is precisely how the pre-FOMC drift and the FOMC-cycle effect got traded after they had already died. The second objection is that Bomfim's sample is 1989-1998 and the Fed's communication regime has changed twice since; the lull's magnitude today is unmeasured.
